Adam [@kingma2015adam] solves a one-dimensional problem, once per coordinate:
*given a noisy gradient, how big a step should I take?* Almost every interesting
training problem today is two-dimensional — fine-tune **and** don't regress,
align **and** stay capable, unlearn **and** keep the accuracy. The standard
answer is to sum the two losses and hand the sum to Adam, which throws away
exactly the information that matters: whether the two objectives actually agreed
on that coordinate, and whether we had enough data to tell.

> Adam's per-coordinate multiplier is a **squashed signal-to-noise ratio**. Once
> you write it that way, the two-objective version is forced: replace the scalar
> soft sign by the probability that the two true gradients *agree in sign*. That
> object is the **focus vector**, and it is a 2D Adam.

The focus vector comes from my paper on unlearning
[@dine2025improving], where it is derived as a masking rule. This post drops the
unlearning and keeps the optimiser, because nothing in it is about forgetting.
It also argues that the same reading fixes something in ordinary 1D Adam: the
square root in the denominator is the wrong squashing function, and $\Phi$ is
the right one.

## Adam is a decision about a sign

Write Adam per coordinate, dropping the bias correction:

$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\,\frac{\hat m_t}{\sqrt{\hat v_t} + \epsilon},
\qquad
\hat m_t = \mathrm{EMA}(\hat g_t), \quad \hat v_t = \mathrm{EMA}(\hat g_t^2).
$$ {#eq-adam}

Model the per-step gradients of coordinate $i$ as $\hat g_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,
\sigma^2)$, i.i.d. — $\mu$ the true gradient, $\sigma$ the estimation noise.
Then $\E[\hat m_t] = \mu$ and $\E[\hat v_t] = \mu^2 + \sigma^2$, so the
multiplier in @eq-adam concentrates on

$$
\frac{\mu}{\sqrt{\mu^2 + \sigma^2}} \;=\; \frac{s}{\sqrt{1+s^2}}
\;=:\; \psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}(s),
\qquad s \doteq \frac{\mu}{\sigma}.
$$ {#eq-psi-adam}

Adam's step size on a coordinate is **a function of that coordinate's
signal-to-noise ratio and nothing else**. This is the variance-adaptation
reading of [@balles2018dissecting]: $\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ is odd, maps $\R \to
(-1,1)$, is linear near the origin and tends to $\pm 1$, so Adam interpolates
between plain SGD at low SNR and signSGD [@bernstein2018signsgd] at high SNR.
The $\epsilon$ in @eq-adam exists only to keep the ratio finite; it is not part
of the idea.

A quick numerical check that @eq-psi-adam is not an artefact of the
approximation — simulating @eq-adam with $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$:

| $s$ | $\E[\hat m/\sqrt{\hat v}]$ (simulated) | $s/\sqrt{1+s^2}$ | $2\Phi(s)-1$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 0.102 | 0.100 | 0.080 |
| 0.5 | 0.456 | 0.447 | 0.383 |
| 1.0 | 0.704 | 0.707 | 0.683 |
| 2.0 | 0.894 | 0.894 | 0.955 |
| 5.0 | 0.980 | 0.981 | 1.000 |

## The squashing should be $\Phi$, not a square root

So Adam is deciding how much to commit to $\operatorname{sign}(\hat g_i)$ given
how noisy the estimate is. That is a statistical question with an answer. Under
the same Gaussian model, with a flat prior on the unknown $\mu$, the posterior
is $\mu \mid \hat g \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat g, \sigma^2)$, hence

$$
\mathbb{P}\!\left[\mu > 0 \mid \hat g\right] = \Phi(s),
\qquad
\E\!\left[\operatorname{sign}(\mu) \mid \hat g\right] = 2\Phi(s) - 1 \;=:\; \psi_\Phi(s),
$$ {#eq-psi-phi}

with $\Phi$ the standard Gaussian CDF. $\psi_\Phi$ has every structural property
of $\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}$ — odd, bounded by $1$, linear at the origin
($\psi_\Phi'(0) = \sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 0.80$ against $1$, a constant that the
learning rate absorbs), sign in the limit — and one that $\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}$
lacks: **it is a probability**. The square root is a guess at the shape of a
function whose exact form the noise model already determines.

::: {.light-content}
![](squashing-light.svg)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](squashing-dark.svg)
:::

*Left: the two squashings against the per-coordinate SNR. Right: how fast each
commits to the sign. Adam's residual doubt decays polynomially, $1 -
\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}(s) \sim 1/2s^2$; the Gaussian CDF's decays like
$e^{-s^2/2}$.*

The difference is entirely in the tail, and it is large. At $s = 4$ — a
coordinate whose sign is not seriously in question — Adam still withholds $3\%$
of the step as if unsure, while $\psi_\Phi$ withholds $0.006\%$. Below $s
\approx 1$ the ordering flips and $\psi_\Phi$ is the more cautious of the two.
Adam is thus simultaneously too timid where the signal is clear and too eager
where it is not, which is precisely the profile you would expect from a
squashing function chosen for algebraic convenience.

## Two objectives: the focus vector

Now the actual point. Take an objective $U$ to minimise and a constraint $C \le
0$ to respect, each with its own batch gradient and its own noise
[@dine2025improving]:

$$
\hat g_U = g_U + N_U, \quad N_U \sim \mathcal{N}(0; \Sigma_U),
\qquad
\hat g_C = g_C + N_C, \quad N_C \sim \mathcal{N}(0; \Sigma_C),
$$ {#eq-model}

with $N_U \perp N_C$. Per coordinate we now have two SNRs, $s_{U,i}$ and
$s_{C,i}$, and therefore two soft signs $\psi_\Phi(s_{U,i})$ and
$\psi_\Phi(s_{C,i})$. A coordinate is safe to move exactly when the two *true*
gradients point the same way, and the probability of that is available in closed
form.

::: {#prp-focus name="the focus vector, and the identity"}

&nbsp;

Write $\varphi_U \doteq \Phi\big(\hat g_U/\sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(\Sigma_U)}\big)$
component-wise, idem for $\varphi_C$. Then

$$
f_i \;\doteq\; \mathbb{P}\!\left[g_{U,i}\,g_{C,i} > 0 \,\middle|\, \hat g_U, \hat g_C\right]
\;=\; \varphi_{U,i}\varphi_{C,i} + (1-\varphi_{U,i})(1-\varphi_{C,i})
$$ {#eq-focus}

and, equivalently,

$$
\boxed{\;f_i \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\Big(1 + \psi_\Phi(s_{U,i})\,\psi_\Phi(s_{C,i})\Big).\;}
$$ {#eq-identity}

:::

@eq-focus is Prop. 4 of [@dine2025improving]. @eq-identity is one line from it:
substituting $\varphi = (1+\psi_\Phi)/2$ into @eq-focus, the linear terms
cancel and only $\tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \psi_\Phi(s_U)\psi_\Phi(s_C))$ survives. But
that line is the whole story of this post. The focus vector is **the product of
two Adam multipliers**, rescaled from $[-1,1]$ to $[0,1]$; equivalently, $2f-1 =
\E[\operatorname{sign}(g_U)\operatorname{sign}(g_C) \mid \hat g_U, \hat g_C]$ is
a per-coordinate *sign correlation* between the two objectives. One-dimensional
Adam asks "which way, and how sure am I?"; the two-dimensional version asks the
same question twice and multiplies the answers.

::: {.light-content}
![](gate-light.png)
:::

::: {.dark-content}
![](gate-dark.png)
:::

*The gate $f$ as a function of the two SNRs. Along either axis one objective
carries no signal and $f = \tfrac{1}{2}$: the coordinate is neither trusted nor
blocked, just half-stepped.*

The update is the aggregate gradient passed through the gate:

$$
\Delta_{\mathrm{F}} \;\doteq\; -\,f \odot \mathrm{Agg}(\hat g_U, \hat g_C),
\qquad
\mathrm{Agg}(x,y) = \alpha x + \beta y, \quad (\alpha,\beta) \in \R_+^2 ,
$$ {#eq-update}

and if you want the version where *every* quantity is a squashed SNR — the pure
2D Adam — feed the aggregate through the same soft sign:

$$
\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\,
\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}\big(1 + \psi_\Phi(s_U)\psi_\Phi(s_C)\big)}_{\text{gate}}
\odot
\underbrace{\big(\alpha\,\psi_\Phi(s_U) + \beta\,\psi_\Phi(s_C)\big)}_{\text{direction}} .
$$ {#eq-2dadam}

### What the gate does at the corners

| regime | $f$ | behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| both variances $\to 0$ | $\{0,1\}$ | the hard AND-mask [@parascandolo2020learning] on the batch gradients |
| both variances $\to \infty$ | $1/2$ | halve the learning rate, change nothing else |
| one objective uninformative | $1/2$ | abstain, half-step |
| $C = U$ (single objective) | $\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\psi_\Phi(s)^2) \in [\tfrac{1}{2},1]$ | 1D Adam with a confidence-modulated step |

The first two lines are Prop. 7 of [@dine2025improving]. Two structural
consequences are worth stating on their own. First, $f \ge 0$ always, so the
gate can attenuate a coordinate but never flip it: unlike projection-based
conflict resolution [@yu2020gradient; @liu2021conflict], the update is a
non-negative reweighting of the aggregate direction and never rotates it into
something the aggregate did not propose. Second, $f$ is bounded in $[0,1]$ by
construction, so the pathology Adam's $\epsilon$ patches — a vanishing
denominator blowing up a step — has no analogue here.

The last line of the table deserves its own name. Applied to a single objective,
@eq-2dadam is Adam whose effective learning rate ranges over $[\eta/2, \eta]$
according to how confident the coordinate is — a strictly milder,
better-motivated variant of the $\epsilon$ hack.

## The guarantees

Gating is only interesting if it still descends. It does, on **both** objectives
at once.

::: {#prp-guarantee name="feasibility in expectation, Prop. 6 of the paper"}

&nbsp;

Let $\mathrm{Agg}$ be the positive combination $\alpha x + \beta y$, $\alpha,
\beta > 0$, and suppose $\E[\langle \hat g_U, \hat g_C\rangle] = 0$. Then for
any sufficiently small $\eta > 0$,

$$
\E\big[U(\theta_0 + \eta \Delta_{\mathrm{F}}(\theta_0))\big] \le U(\theta_0),
\qquad
\E\big[C(\theta_0 + \eta \Delta_{\mathrm{F}}(\theta_0))\big] \le 0 .
$$ {#eq-guarantee}

:::

The mechanism is visible in one expansion. Descent on $U$ needs $\langle
\Delta_{\mathrm{F}}, \hat g_U\rangle \le 0$, i.e.

$$
\alpha \sum_i f_i\, \hat g_{U,i}^2 \;+\; \beta \sum_i f_i\, \hat g_{U,i}\hat g_{C,i}
\;\ge\; 0 .
$$ {#eq-expansion}

The first sum is non-negative for free, because $f \ge 0$ — that is the whole
value of a gate that cannot change signs. Only the cross term needs an argument,
and the paper supplies the cheapest one available: two random vectors in high
dimension have vanishing inner product, and empirically $\langle \hat g_U, \hat
g_C\rangle$ sits around $\pm 10^{-5}$ at the start and decays to $\pm 10^{-10}$.

The assumption is in fact stronger than necessary, and in a direction worth
noting. The cross term in @eq-expansion is not the plain inner product but the
$f$-weighted one, and $f$ is by construction *large exactly where the product
$\hat g_{U,i}\hat g_{C,i}$ is positive*. The weighting is positively associated
with what it weights, so the sum should be biased upward rather than merely
vanish. A quick simulation — $d = 4000$ coordinates, true gradients drawn
independently, heterogeneous noise scales, $600$ draws — is unambiguous:

```python
phi_U, phi_C = norm.cdf(gh_U / s_U), norm.cdf(gh_C / s_C)
f = phi_U * phi_C + (1 - phi_U) * (1 - phi_C)
cross_weighted = np.sum(f * gh_U * gh_C)   # > 0 in 600 / 600 draws
cross_plain    = np.dot(gh_U, gh_C)        # straddles 0, mean ~ 0
```

The unweighted inner product straddles zero as advertised; the $f$-weighted one
was positive in every single draw, and both $\langle g_U,
\Delta_{\mathrm{F}}\rangle$ and $\langle g_C, \Delta_{\mathrm{F}}\rangle$ were
negative in every draw. So @prp-guarantee holds with room to spare, and the
honest statement is that the focus weighting *helps* the guarantee instead of
needing an assumption to survive it. Turning "positively associated" into a
proof — an FKG-type inequality on the concordance of $f$ with $\hat g_U \odot
\hat g_C$ — is open.

There is also a trust region. With $\Delta = -m \odot \mathrm{Agg}$, for all $q
\ge 1$,

$$
\|\theta - \theta_0\|_q \;\le\; \eta\,\big\|m(\nabla U, \nabla C)(\theta_0)\big\|_0^{1/q}\,
\big\|\Delta(\theta_0)\big\|_\infty ,
$$ {#eq-vicinity}

so the step is controlled by how many coordinates the gate opens — and in
practice that number falls as training proceeds.

## What I would change next

Writing the method as an optimiser exposes a soft spot in its own
implementation. Algorithm 1 of [@dine2025improving] estimates
$\sqrt{\mathrm{diag}(\Sigma)}$ by reading off Adam's second moment $\hat v$,
which is free and convenient. But $\hat v$ estimates $\mu^2 + \sigma^2$, not
$\sigma^2$, and it is the noise of a *single datum*, not of the batch mean. Two
consequences:

1. **Feeding a squashed quantity into a squashing function.** The argument
   handed to $\Phi$ is close to $\psi_{\mathrm{Adam}}(s)$, an $O(1)$ number, so
   $\varphi$ rarely leaves $(\Phi(-1), \Phi(1)) = (0.16, 0.84)$ and $f$ rarely
   leaves $(0.27, 0.73)$. The gate is real but it is being applied at low
   contrast. The fix is to divide by an estimate of $\sigma$ alone — the
   AdaBelief statistic $\hat v - \hat m^2$ [@zhuang2020adabelief] — so the SNR
   handed to $\Phi$ is unbounded and the gate can actually saturate.
2. **Blindness to batch size.** The estimation noise on a mean of $B$ samples is
   $\sigma/\sqrt{B}$, so the correct argument is $\sqrt{B}\,\hat g/\hat\sigma$.
   As written, doubling the batch buys no extra confidence — which is exactly
   the quantity the method claims to reason about.

Both fixes point at the same replacement, $\varphi \leftarrow
\Phi\big(\lambda\sqrt{B}\,\hat g/\sqrt{\hat v - \hat m^2}\big)$, with $\lambda$
a temperature. At $B = 256$ the $\sqrt{B} = 16$ factor will saturate the gate
into the hard AND-mask, so $\lambda$ is doing real work — but it is one
interpretable hyperparameter replacing the certainty threshold $p$, on a scale
where $\lambda = 1$ is the statistically honest setting and everything else is a
deliberate hedge against the Gaussian model being wrong.

## Open questions

- **Q1. More than two objectives.** The closed form generalises immediately:
  $\mathbb{P}[\text{all } n \text{ agree}] = \prod_k \varphi_k + \prod_k (1 -
  \varphi_k)$, which decays to $2^{1-n}$ and gates everything shut for moderate
  $n$. Pairwise gates, or a soft-OR over pairs, are the obvious repairs; which
  one keeps @prp-guarantee is not obvious.
- **Q2. Proving the association.** Does $\mathrm{Cov}(f_i, \hat g_{U,i}\hat
  g_{C,i}) \ge 0$ hold in general under @eq-model? Simulation says yes,
  emphatically; a proof would let @prp-guarantee drop its hypothesis entirely.
- **Q3. Does $\Phi$ beat the square root in plain 1D training?** The tail
  argument says a $\Phi$-Adam should behave like signSGD sooner. That is a
  cheap experiment on a standard benchmark and I have not run it.
- **Q4. Beyond Gaussian.** @eq-model is the one modelling choice in the whole
  construction, and gradient noise is famously heavier-tailed. Swapping $\Phi$
  for a Student-$t$ CDF changes nothing structurally — @eq-identity survives any
  symmetric noise family — but it changes the tail, which is where all the
  action is.
